title: The Baby and the Marriage
text:
The arrival of a first baby is a joy, but many couples find that their marriage becomes harder afterward. Alyson Shapiro, John Gottman and Sybil Carrere at the University of Washington wanted to know why some marriages weather the transition better than others.

They drew on a group of newlywed couples in the Seattle area whom Gottman's lab had been following since early in their marriages. Some of these couples had a first child over the next several years; others did not. Because the researchers had interviewed and observed the couples before any baby arrived, they could look for early signs that predicted what happened afterward.

Among the couples who became parents, about two-thirds of the wives reported a drop in marital satisfaction during the first years with the baby. The other third stayed stable or even grew happier. The couples who did not have children did not show the same decline over the same period.

What set the protected couples apart was visible before the birth. Husbands who expressed fondness and admiration for their wives, and who were aware of and interested in their wives' lives and the details of their world, predicted stable or rising satisfaction for the wives. Couples who described their lives as chaotic and out of control fared worse.
lesson: Before and after a baby arrives, keep showing fondness for your partner and stay curious about their inner world. That habit protects the marriage through hard years.
people: Alyson Shapiro, John Gottman, Sybil Carrere
source: Shapiro, A. F., Gottman, J. M., and Carrere, S. (2000). The baby and the marriage: Identifying factors that buffer against decline in marital satisfaction after the first baby arrives. Journal of Family Psychology, 14(1), 59-70.
